questions.q: Sort these into time rows — past, present, future: 'She has finished', 'She will be finishing', 'She had finished'.
questions.a: 'She has finished' → present (perfect aspect anchors it to now). 'She will be finishing' → future. 'She had finished' → past. A wrong answer putting 'has finished' in the past reveals the student reads the participle 'finished' as the tense carrier instead of the auxiliary 'has' — the tense lives in the helper, not the main verb.

questions.q: Change ONLY the aspect, keep the time: 'He played cricket' → two other past forms.
questions.a: 'He was playing cricket' (continuous) and 'He had played cricket' (perfect). A wrong answer like 'he plays' or 'he will play' shows the student changed the TIME row, not the aspect column — they cannot yet decouple the two axes, which is the whole point of the grid.

questions.q: Which form fits: 'At this moment, the baby ___ (cry).' Defend your choice.
questions.a: 'is crying' — present continuous, because 'at this moment' marks an ongoing action in present time. A wrong answer 'cries' or 'is cried' reveals the student matches tense to the verb's dictionary feel rather than to the time-marker in the sentence.

questions.q: English has exactly twelve tense forms — three times (present, past, future) crossed with four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, ______).
Fill in the blank: ______ has exactly twelve tense forms — three times (present, past, future) crossed with four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect-continuous).
Fill in the blank: Draw the grid on the board: rows = time, columns = ______.
What is English has exactly twelve tense forms? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: English has exactly twelve tense forms — three times (present, past, future) crossed with four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect-continuous).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about English has exactly twelve tense forms?
questions.a: Students believe the tense name describes the verb alone ('wrote = past tense of write') and miss that aspect — the helper verbs — carries half the meaning.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can place any given verb phrase into the correct cell of the 3×4 tense grid, name its time and aspect, and produce the same meaning in at least two other cells on demand.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Draw the grid on the board: rows = time, ______ = aspect.
